newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil proposes wider land reform as protest looms.
newsitem.headline: Brazil proposes wider land reform as protest looms.

text.p: The Brazilian government on Wednesday said it would offer to widen its land reform programme when demonstrators from the radical Landless Movement (MST) reach Brasilia on Thursday after a two-month protest march.

About 1,500 ragged marchers were already in cities surrounding the capital and agrarian reform minister Raul Jungmann said the government was drawing up a new credit system that would offer loans to recently settled families.
"It would be a revolution," Jungmann said, adding that settlers currently have no access to credit for setting up their own farm or business or buying land.

A senior official also said the government was willing to increase its target of settling 280,000 families during its four-year term, but only on the condition the MST suspends its controversial and often violent invasions of private farmland.
"If the MST is willing to stop its invasions then the government is willing to make progress," said the official, who asked not to be named.

The proposals came on the eve of what could be the biggest protest of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's term. The landless peasants, toting farm tools and revolutionary-looking red flags, were to march into the capital and demonstrate in front of the presidential palace, ending a 750-mile (1,200-km) trek for faster land reform.

The MST said nearly five million families need their own land as an alternative to the squalor of urban shantytowns or the poverty of life as casual labourers in the countryside. About half of Brazil's farmland belongs to just 2 percent of landowners, one of the world's worst land distribution ratios.
Thursday also marks the first anniversary of a massacre by police of 19 rural labourers on a remote Amazon highway. No one has been arrested in connection with the killing.

Tens of thousands of workers from CUT union confederation, Brazil's largest labour group, were expected to swell the ranks and call on the government to halt its privatisation programme and scrap reforms to streamline the state.

Cardoso has agreed to meet the MST's leadership on Friday in the first top-level talks since last August when the government refused to negotiate with the movement as long as it continued to invade private land. With public opinion on the MST's side -- a recent poll found 85 percent of Brazilians supported non-violent invasions -- the government has been forced to change its tune.

"Until last month the government refused to talk to the MST about land reform," Luiz Eduardo Greenhalgh, MST lawyer and a member of the Chamber of Deputies in Congress, said. "There has been a radical turnaround in official policy."
